lines.text: Okay, so. Picture a sheet of squared paper and a pen, and you want to draw a shape out of little stars. The sheet’s six squares across and six rows down.
Here’s what we’re after. Before we write anything, just count the stars on each row with me. Six. Four. Two. Two. Four. Six.
See how they mirror each other? Top row and bottom row match. Second one and second from last match. And the two in the middle are twins.
So what’s actually changing? Only one thing. How many squares we leave empty at each side. None at the top. One as you come in. Two in the middle.
And that’s it, honestly. That’s the whole trick. Work out that one number for a row, and the row draws itself.
Right. Let’s write it down.
Before we run anything, let’s learn to read it. None of this is magic. It’s all shorthand, and every bit of it means something plain.
This little word tells the computer what kind of thing we’re about to keep. Int is short for integer, which just means a whole number. No halves, no decimals.
And n is just a name we invented. We could have called it size, or sheet, or anything. We need a name so we can point at it again later.

Now this one catches everybody out. That equals sign does not mean ‘is equal to’, the way it does in maths. It means: put this into that. Read the whole line as ‘make a box called n, and put six in it’.
And the semicolon is simply a full stop. It says: that instruction is finished, you can move on.
Right. This line looks like a lot at once. It really isn’t. Let’s take it apart piece by piece.
For just means: do this again and again. That’s the whole word. It’s the computer’s way of saying ‘keep repeating’.
The round brackets hold the settings for the repeating. Think of the dials on a machine that you set before you switch it on.
First dial: where to start. This sets up a counter and puts zero in it. Zero, not one, because computers count from zero. You do get used to it.
Second dial: when to stop. That little arrow pointing left means ‘smaller than’. So this says: keep going for as long as the counter hasn’t reached six yet.
Third dial: what to do after each turn. Those two plus signs just mean ‘add one’. One more, every time round.
And the curly bracket opens a box. Everything inside that box happens on every single turn of the loop.

Now look at where this next line starts. It sits further to the right than the one above it. That gap is not decoration. It means this line lives inside the loop above. The further right something sits, the deeper inside it is. It’s written that way for you, not for the computer.
Math dot min is a little helper that comes with the language. You hand it two numbers, and it hands you back the smaller of the two. That is genuinely all it does.
And this is just arithmetic, read out loud: six, take away one, take away whatever row we are on.
Print puts something on the screen and stays where it is, on the same line. Its cousin println prints and then drops to a new line. That is the only difference between them.
That’s the whole alphabet. Now let’s watch it being written.
First line’s easy. It just says how big the sheet is. Six by six.
Now this one. It’s how we walk down the rows, one after another, starting at row zero. Computers count from zero, not one. You get used to it.
And this does the same thing sideways. For each row, it walks across the squares, left to right.
Now, this line looks scary. It isn’t. It’s just working out that number we found a minute ago, how far in from the edge we are. That’s all edge means.
And here’s the decision. Read it out loud with me: put a star if we’re past the left border and, at the same time, before the right one. Otherwise, leave a gap.
Last bit just says: row’s finished, go to the next line.
Right, let’s watch it go.
Row zero. There’s nothing to skip here, so it fills straight across. Six stars.
Row’s done, so the pen hops back to the left and drops down a line. Like pressing Enter.
Row one now. We skip one square at each end, so that leaves four in the middle.
See? It skips this one, because edge is one now.
And from here it fills, all the way to the second from last.
Row two. Two skipped on each side this time, and we’re down to a pair.
Row three. Same as the one above it, so this is the waist. From here it opens back out.
Row four. Back to skipping just one, so we’re at four again, like row one.
And the last row is full, exactly like the first. There’s your hourglass.
And there it is. Want to see how you’d change it to make a diamond instead?
Same size.
Same rows, and the same number as before.
But now, instead of asking, we just walk past that many squares.
And then lay down exactly the right number of stars.
New line. No questions were asked anywhere.
Watch how different this feels, even though you end up with the same picture.
Row zero. There’s nothing to skip here, so it fills straight across. Six stars. Nothing to skip.
And now the stars, exactly as many as we counted.
Notice the squares at the end. We never even went there.
Row one now. We skip one square at each end, so that leaves four in the middle. Skip 1, then draw 4.
Walking past, counting. No decision to make.
Row two. Two skipped on each side this time, and we’re down to a pair. Skip 2, then draw 2.
Row three. Same as the one above it, so this is the waist. From here it opens back out. Skip 2, then draw 2.
Row four. Back to skipping just one, so we’re at four again, like row one. Skip 1, then draw 4.
And the last row is full, exactly like the first. There’s your hourglass. Nothing to skip.
Same hourglass, and we never asked a single question. We just counted.
The rows, and the same number as always.
The sweep across the row.
And here the question and the answer are squeezed onto a single line.
New line. Shorter to read, but nothing has really changed.
Same decisions as before. It’s only the writing that got shorter.
The whole test lives inside the print. Ask and answer in one breath.
Inside the band.
And out again.
Fewer lines to read, sure. But the computer did exactly the same work. Short isn’t the same as fast.
The rows, and the same number.
And here we never sweep at all. We ask for the whole line, ready made.
That is the entire program.
Keep an eye on the counter for this one. It barely moves.
And the whole line lands at once, like pressing a stamp.
Last one. Six lines, six steps.
Same picture, a handful of steps. The work didn’t vanish, though. Somebody else wrote it once, so you don’t have to.
